title: Informed search
summary: Greedy best-first follows h alone and is not optimal. A* follows f=g+h, and it is optimal on trees when h is admissible and on graphs when h is consistent.
intuition:
Informed search ranks nodes with a heuristic $h(n)$, an estimate of the cheapest remaining cost from $n$ to a goal. Greedy best-first search uses that estimate alone: its priority is $f=h$. It runs toward whatever looks closest. Nothing in that rule accounts for the cost already spent, so a cheap-looking branch can hide an expensive finish, and the path it returns need not be optimal.

A* adds the cost already spent. The priority is $f(n)=g(n)+h(n)$, where $g(n)$ is the path cost from the start to $n$. If $h$ never overestimates the true remaining cost $h^*$, A* on a tree returns an optimal path: a node on the optimal path is expanded before any goal whose $f$ is worse than the optimum. That property is admissibility, $h(n)\le h^*(n)$ for every $n$, together with $h(\mathrm{goal})=0$.

$$
f(n)=g(n)+h(n)
$$

Graph search is stricter, because a state can be reached by more than one path and a closed node is not reopened. The hypothesis that makes A* graph search optimal is consistency: $h(n)\le c(n,a,n')+h(n')$ for every edge. Consistency implies admissibility when $h$ at a goal is $0$, by chaining the inequality along an optimal path. An inadmissible heuristic is outside both theorems. A* with such an $h$ can return a suboptimal path, and the lesson's second trace is one place it does.

definitions.body: A heuristic with $h(n)\le h^*(n)$ for every node, where $h^*(n)$ is the true cheapest cost from $n$ to a goal. It never overestimates. This is enough for optimal A* tree search.
A heuristic with $h(n)\le c(n,a,n')+h(n')$ on every edge. It is the hypothesis for optimal A* graph search. If $h(\mathrm{goal})=0$, consistency implies admissibility.
Search that expands the open node with the smallest $h$. It uses $f=h$ and ignores $g$. It is not an optimal algorithm.
$g(n)$ is the cost from the start along the current path, $h(n)$ estimates the cost onward, and A* sorts by $f(n)=g(n)+h(n)$.

formulas.name: A* priority
formulas.note: Greedy best-first drops $g$ and sorts by $h$ alone. That version is not optimal.

formulas.name: Admissibility
formulas.note: Never overestimate the remaining cost. Enough for optimal tree search, with $h$ at a goal equal to $0$.

formulas.name: Consistency
formulas.note: A triangle inequality on every edge. Implies admissibility when $h(\mathrm{goal})=0$, and it is the hypothesis for optimal graph search.

properties: Greedy best-first uses $f=h$ only. It is not optimal. On the five-node graph below it returns cost $6$ when the optimum is $4$.
A* uses $f=g+h$. Admissible $h$, with $h(\mathrm{goal})=0$, makes tree search optimal.
Consistent $h$ makes graph search optimal. The first time a state is expanded, its $g$ is already the best $g$.
Consistency implies admissibility when the heuristic is $0$ at every goal: chain $h(n)\le c+h(n')$ along an optimal path.
If some $h(n)>h^*(n)$, the optimality theorems do not apply. The modified trace with $h(C)=5$ returns cost $6$.

examples.title: A* on a five-node graph
examples.prompt: Nodes are $S,A,B,C,G$. Edges: $S\xrightarrow{1}A$, $S\xrightarrow{4}B$, $A\xrightarrow{2}C$, $A\xrightarrow{3}B$, $B\xrightarrow{2}G$, $C\xrightarrow{1}G$. Heuristic: $h(S)=3$, $h(A)=2$, $h(B)=1$, $h(C)=1$, $h(G)=0$. Run A* graph search, breaking no ties because each chosen $f$ is strictly smaller than the other open $f$ values.
steps: The true remaining costs are $h^*(C)=1$, $h^*(B)=2$, $h^*(A)=3$ via $A-C-G$ (the path $A-B-G$ costs $5$), and $h^*(S)=4$ via $S-A-C-G$ (the path $S-B-G$ costs $6$). Every given $h(n)$ is at most $h^*(n)$, so $h$ is admissible. It is also consistent: for example $h(S)=3\le 1+h(A)=3$ and $h(A)=2\le 2+h(C)=3$.
Start at $S$ with $g=0$, $f=3$. The children are $A$ at $g=1$, $h=2$, $f=3$ and $B$ at $g=4$, $h=1$, $f=5$. Expand $A$.
From $A$, $C$ has $g=3$, $h=1$, $f=4$. The path $S-A-B$ has $g=4$, which does not beat the copy of $B$ already stored at $g=4$. Expand $C$, the open node with smallest $f$.
From $C$, $G$ has $g=4$, $h=0$, $f=4$. The other open node is $B$ at $f=5$. Expand $G$. The path $S-A-C-G$ costs $4$, and every remaining open $f$ is at least $4$, with $B$ strictly worse.
examples.answer: A* expands $S,A,C,G$ in that order and returns cost $4$. $B$ is never expanded.

examples.title: Greedy is not optimal, and an overestimate is outside the theorem
examples.prompt: On the same graph, run greedy best-first using only $h$. Then change the heuristic at $C$ to $5$ and run A* again.
steps: Greedy best-first expands $S$ and compares children by $h$ alone. $h(B)=1$ is smaller than $h(A)=2$, so it expands $B$ and then $G$.
The path $S-B-G$ costs $4+2=6$. The optimal path $S-A-C-G$ costs $4$, so this greedy run is not optimal.
Now set $h(C)=5$. That is larger than $h^*(C)=1$, so the heuristic is inadmissible. A* expands $S$ ($f=3$), then $A$ ($f=3$). The child $C$ has $g=3$ and $f=3+5=8$.

$B$ has $f=5$, so A* expands $B$ and generates $G$ at $g=6$, $f=6$. That $f$ is smaller than $8$, so $G$ is expanded at cost $6$ and $C$ is never expanded. The returned cost is not optimal. Admissibility was the hypothesis that failed.
examples.answer: Greedy best-first returns cost $6$. A* with the inadmissible value $h(C)=5$ also returns cost $6$, by the expansion order $S,A,B,G$.

traps: Sorting by $h$ and calling the algorithm A*. A* adds $g$. The version that uses $h$ alone is greedy best-first, and it is not optimal.
Using admissibility as the hypothesis for graph search that never reopens a closed node. That hypothesis is consistency.
Claiming A* is optimal for an inadmissible heuristic. The run with $h(C)=5$ returns $6$ on a graph whose optimum is $4$.
Forgetting that consistency implies admissibility only with the goal condition. The chaining argument ends at $h(\mathrm{goal})=0$.
Treating a tie in $f$ as a change in the optimum. Ties can change the expansion order. They do not change the cost once $h$ is admissible on a tree, or consistent on a graph.

questions.stem: On the graph with edges $S\xrightarrow{1}A$, $S\xrightarrow{4}B$, $A\xrightarrow{2}C$, $A\xrightarrow{3}B$, $B\xrightarrow{2}G$, $C\xrightarrow{1}G$ and heuristic $h(S)=3$, $h(A)=2$, $h(B)=1$, $h(C)=1$, $h(G)=0$, A* graph search returns
questions.solution: The answer is **B**. $f(S)=3$, $f(A)=3$, $f(B)=5$, $f(C)=4$, and $f(G)=4$ along $S-A-C-G$. The open node with strictly smallest $f$ is $A$, then $C$, then $G$, and $B$ stays at $f=5$. The path cost is $1+2+1=4$. Option A is the greedy path.

questions.stem: Greedy best-first search on that same graph, using $f=h$ only, returns
questions.solution: The answer is **B**, cost $6$ along $S-B-G$. From $S$ the heuristic prefers $B$ because $h(B)=1<h(A)=2$, and $B$'s child is $G$. The path cost is $4+2=6$. The optimal cost is $4$, so this is a concrete case where $f=h$ is not optimal.

questions.stem: For the same five-node graph, $h^*(S)=4$, $h^*(A)=3$, $h^*(B)=2$, $h^*(C)=1$, and $h^*(G)=0$. The heuristic in the lesson is $3,2,1,1,0$ at $S,A,B,C,G$. Which of the following are true?
options: A* with $h(C)=5$ and the other heuristic values unchanged returns cost $6$.
Consistency is the hypothesis used for optimal A* graph search.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, C, and D**. Each lesson value is at most the corresponding $h^*$, so the heuristic is admissible; $h(C)=5>1$, so B is false. With that overestimate, $f(C)=8$ and A* expands $G$ through $B$ at cost $6$. Optimal graph search is stated under consistency, which this admissible heuristic also satisfies, but the implication used in D is the general one.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: An admissible heuristic is enough for optimal A* tree search.
Greedy best-first uses $f=h$ and is not optimal in general.
A consistent heuristic with $h(\mathrm{goal})=0$ is admissible.
A* sorts open nodes by $h$ alone.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and C**. Tree search does not reuse a state along another path, and admissibility is the hypothesis that keeps the optimal path ahead of a suboptimal goal. Greedy best-first really does drop $g$, which is why D is false: A* sorts by $g+h$. Chaining the consistency inequality along an optimal path yields $h(n)\le h^*(n)$ when the goal heuristic is $0$.

questions.stem: A second graph has edges $S\xrightarrow{4}A\xrightarrow{5}G$, $S\xrightarrow{6}B\xrightarrow{4}G$, and $S\xrightarrow{3}C\xrightarrow{8}G$. Every step cost is positive, and an admissible heuristic is available to A*. Enter the optimal path cost.
questions.solution: The answer is **9**. The three paths cost $4+5=9$, $6+4=10$, and $3+8=11$. The minimum is $9$, along $S-A-G$. Admissibility is what lets A* tree search return that minimum; the number itself is the shortest path.
